query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing to inherit microstructural lamellae in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will simultaneously increase strength and ductility due to the two-hierarchical constraint effect and self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
generation.intervention: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing to inherit microstructural lamellae
generation.mechanism: Two-hierarchical constraint effect and self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism
generation.uncertainty: Difficulty in controlling the processing conditions to achieve the desired microstructure

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy processed with tailored thermo-mechanical processing to those processed with conventional methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored thermo-mechanical processing does not result in improved strength and ductility compared to conventional methods, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. Producing in situ composite materials with superior strength and ductility has long been a challenge. Here, the authors use lamellar microstructure inherited from casting, rol

In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). However, dynamic strengthening mechanisms and phase interactions during external loading is not well understood for these eutectic alloys. The large fraction of phase boundary significantly impacts plastic flow in these systems. Considering the effect of thermo-mechanical processing on tailoring the microstructure and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, understanding of phase-specific mechanical response is critical for fundamental insights as well as wider application of these alloys. Here, phase-specific mechanical behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy was evaluated for better understanding of phase boundary interactions during loading. Measurement of hardness, modulus, strain rate sensitivity, yielding and plastic deformation of micro-pillars, and friction analysis was done at the microstructural length-scale and compared with bulk mechanical response. This will pave the way for designing stronger and tougher complex phase HEAs.

decision.rationale: Direction A is chosen because it directly addresses the limitation of simultaneously increasing strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys by proposing tailored thermo-mechanical processing to inherit microstructural lamellae. The critic's review suggests that the proposed mechanism is physically sound, and the supplied records provide evidence to support the intervention.
